missions.name: Expanding Codes with Polynomial Stretch
missions.description:
## Why expansion does not settle noisy-codeword detection

A collection of sparse parity equations can involve almost as many variables as its total number of variable occurrences. This **expansion** property excludes small linear dependencies and is relevant to the complexity of recognizing noisy planted equations. It is therefore useful to distinguish what expansion guarantees from what it leaves possible. Hair and Sahai construct expanding binary matrices for which every sufficiently low-weight corruption of every codeword is recognizable in polynomial time. The result permits constant row weight, polynomially many equations and any fixed corruption fraction strictly below one half. These are simultaneous guarantees of [Theorem 1.1 in the October 2026 submission](../../source.pdf), printed page 2.

The question concerns particular structured expanding matrices. It does not assert that recognizing noisy codewords is easy for a uniformly random sparse matrix. The source also studies cryptographic applications and other lower bounds, but the mathematical target here is the unconditional construction and its complete seven-result dependency chain.

## Binary generators and their auxiliary evaluation code

A **binary generator matrix** is an array $G\in\mathbb F_2^{m\times n}$, where addition is modulo two. A message is a column vector $x\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and its codeword is $Gx$. The columns need not be independent. An error is any vector $e\in\mathbb F_2^m$; its **support** is the set of coordinates at which it is nonzero, and its weight is the support's cardinality.

For a row set $S$, let $\Gamma_G(S)$ be the columns containing a nonzero entry in at least one row of $S$. The matrix is **$(\gamma,k,t)$-expanding** if every row has exactly $k$ nonzero entries and $|\Gamma_G(S)|\ge\gamma k|S|$ whenever $|S|\le t$. The empty set is included. A test returns one to accept a received word as a noisy codeword. It need not recover the message.

The specified construction uses a finite field $F_q$ of characteristic two and a fixed public ordering of its $d$-dimensional point set. There are $m=q^d$ rows. Its **generalized Reed–Muller code** $\operatorname{RM}_q(d,R)$ consists of polynomial evaluation tables on all of $F_q^d$, with total degree at most $R$ and each individual degree at most $q-1$, following the generalized evaluation-code setting of [Delsarte, Goethals and MacWilliams](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-9958(70)90214-7). Set $R=\lfloor((d-3)(q-1)-1)/2\rfloor$ and let $V$ evaluate all the reduced monomials of degree at most $R$ in public row order. The **rank test** uses

$$\mathcal M(y)=V\operatorname{diag}(y)V^{\mathsf T},\qquad D(y)=\mathbf1[\operatorname{rank}_{F_q}\mathcal M(y)\le(1/2-\varepsilon/2)m].$$

Binary inputs are embedded as zero and one in $F_q$. Both the rank and the auxiliary code dimension are over $F_q$.

## Formalization targets

For every real $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, the goal is an arity $k=O(\varepsilon^{-6})$, a deterministic row count $m=m(n)$ and fixed sampler and test algorithms such that, eventually in $n$,

$$n<m<n^k,\qquad \Pr[G\text{ is }(1-\varepsilon,k,n^{1-\varepsilon})\text{-expanding}]\ge1-n^{-1/\varepsilon}.$$

Every output has row weight exactly $k$. The sampler takes $\operatorname{poly}_\varepsilon(n)$ time. The deterministic test takes $\operatorname{poly}_\varepsilon(m,n)$ time and, for every output matrix, satisfies

$$|\operatorname{supp}(e)|\le(1/2-\varepsilon)m\ \Longrightarrow\ D(Gx+e)=1,\qquad \Pr[D(U_m)=1]\le e^{-\varepsilon^2m/128}.$$

Here $U_m$ is uniform on every binary word of length $m$. The displayed exponential constant instantiates the source's $\exp(-\Omega_\varepsilon(m))$ using its proof and the rational construction parameter described below. The arity constant is absolute; runtime constants and the eventual threshold depend only on the fixed $\varepsilon$ and its witnesses.

Theorem 2.1 additionally specifies $d=O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ and $m=n^{2d^2+o(1)}$. Its milestones are codeword annihilation and the error-rank bound (Lemma 2.2); ambiguity for varying-alphabet doubly transitive code families (Lemma 2.3); the exact limiting rate and half-erasure ambiguity (Lemma 2.4); arbitrary-error and Bernoulli-error detection (Proposition 2.5); and the two expansion estimates (Lemmas 2.6 and 2.7). All are targets at their source strength.

## What the construction establishes

The result separates strong small-set expansion from the inability to recognize noisy codewords efficiently. It retains this separation with constant locality and polynomial stretch, while permitting adversarial errors arbitrarily close to one half. The guarantee applies even to rare nonexpanding outputs of the sampler. Error locations may depend on the matrix and the message. These distinctions are explicit in [the source's model and main theorem](../../source.pdf), printed pages 1–2.

The formal development would establish the complete known result, including its algorithmic clauses. It would also provide reusable generalized polynomial-evaluation spaces, ambiguity subspaces and a varying-alphabet symmetry theorem. The latter uses the erasure-capacity literature represented by [Kudekar and coauthors](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.04689). The local theorem declarations are proof targets; their compilation does not constitute machine-checked proofs of these results.

## Where the difficulty lies

Exact row weight gives no expansion guarantee for a collection of rows: many incidences may reach the same columns. Combining columns can introduce further losses. Conversely, counting codewords does not provide an efficient test for their neighborhoods under arbitrary corruption. The required test must accept every bounded-weight error while rejecting almost every uniform input, with a positive exponential rate fixed before the input size. A vanishing error probability alone would not give this assertion.

The auxiliary code has growing alphabet and rate strictly below, but close to, one half. Replacing it by a binary Boolean-cube evaluation code changes the problem. Likewise, erasure ambiguity concerns the dimension of words supported on erased coordinates, rather than the dimension of a punctured code or simultaneous recovery of all erased positions. The exact distinctions and limiting-rate formula are part of [Section 2.2](../../source.pdf), printed pages 9–11.

## Formalization scope

Binary vectors use finite coordinate types and matrices act on columns. Each field is a genuine finite characteristic-two field, equipped with public element and row enumerations. Random linear coefficients are independent for each layer and each level set. Hashes are uniform over all functions, independent across layers and of the coefficients. No rank, biregularity, column-independence or successful-expansion condition is inserted into this data.

Finite probability masses and erasure expectations are explicit sums. The continuous-uniform rate is Lebesgue volume inside the unit cube. Real powers preserve the nonintegral expansion cutoff and failure exponent. Both little-o failure estimates remain limits; the hashing estimate is uniform over every admissible preliminary output.

To obtain finite programs for every external real $\varepsilon$, the existential construction chooses a fixed rational $\theta$ with $\varepsilon/2<\theta<\varepsilon$. It uses the specified sampler and exact rational-threshold rank test at $\theta$, retaining all external $\varepsilon$ guarantees. The source proof's rate $\theta^2/32$ yields $\varepsilon^2/128$. The factors of at most four and sixty-four in the dimension and arity bounds preserve their absolute orders.

Runtime means actual transitions of fixed finite Turing machines, including writing the matrix and performing the entire test. The sampler's tape has the computable polynomial step-budget length and consists of unbiased bits. The tester receives the size and ordered word, without a seed or transcript. Correctness and efficient realization are conclusions to prove. A vacuous expansion hypothesis, a fixed alphabet, rational-only external parameters or an assumed rank bound would not satisfy the target. Contributions toward the complete statements, reusable code theory and finite-machine implementations are in scope.

## Selected references

- Isaac M Hair and Amit Sahai, *Expanding Codes with Polynomial Stretch*, STOC 2027 submission #824, October 2026. [Pinned submission PDF](../../source.pdf), especially Theorems 1.1 and 2.1 and Section 2.
- Philippe Delsarte, Jean-Marie Goethals and F. Jessie MacWilliams, *On Generalized Reed–Muller Codes and Their Relatives*, Information and Control 16, 403–442, 1970. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-9958(70)90214-7).
- Shrinivas Kudekar, Santhosh Kumar, Marco Mondelli, Henry D. Pfister, Eren Şaşoğlu and Rüdiger Urbanke, *Reed–Muller Codes Achieve Capacity on Erasure Channels*, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 63(7), 4298–4316, 2017. [Author preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.04689).

main_theorem.theorem_title: Theorem 1.1 — sparse expanding codes with polynomial stretch and arbitrary near-half errors
main_theorem.formal_statement:
namespace ExpandingCodes.PolynomialStretch

/-- Theorem 1.1: constant arity, polynomial stretch and runtime, and the unconditional
near-half arbitrary-error test. The absolute arity constant precedes ε. -/
theorem expanding_codes :
    ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ε < 1 / 2 →
      ∃ (k : ℕ) (m : ℕ → ℕ) (P : ∀ n, PMF (Generator (m n) n))
        (D : ∀ n, Word (m n) → Bool),
        (k : ℝ) ≤ C * ε⁻¹ ^ 6 ∧ EfficientFamily ε k m P D := by sorry

end ExpandingCodes.PolynomialStretch
main_theorem.natural_language_statement:
There is an absolute constant $C>0$ such that for every real $0<\varepsilon<1/2$ there are an integer $k\le C\varepsilon^{-6}$, a deterministic row-count function $m(n)$, a randomized matrix sampler and a deterministic test $D$. For every sufficiently large $n$,
$$n<m(n)<n^k,\qquad m(n)=n^{O_\varepsilon(1)}.$$
The sampler runs in $\operatorname{poly}_\varepsilon(n)$ time on every unbiased random tape, with exactly the stated output law on binary matrices $G\in\mathbb F_2^{m(n)\times n}$. Every output has row weight exactly $k$, and
$$\Pr[G\text{ is }(1-\varepsilon,k,n^{1-\varepsilon})\text{-expanding}]\ge1-n^{-1/\varepsilon}.$$
The test runs in deterministic $\operatorname{poly}_\varepsilon(m,n)$ time. For every sampler output, every binary message $x$ and every binary error $e$ with $|\operatorname{supp}(e)|\le(1/2-\varepsilon)m$,
$$D(Gx+e)=1,\qquad\Pr[D(U_m)=1]\le\exp(-\varepsilon^2m/128).$$
The error may depend arbitrarily on the message and on the sampled matrix. Constants, programs and the eventual size threshold are fixed before $n$, the matrix and its random bits; $k$ does not depend on $n$.

This is the headline existence theorem. The construction milestone supplies its witnesses without restricting $\varepsilon$ to rational values or assuming successful expansion.

Differences from the source:
- encoding: randomized polynomial-time sampler and deterministic polynomial-time test → fixed finite transition tables, a polynomial-length unbiased tape, exact output law, and worst-case transition bounds; reason: this spells out the algorithmic existence clauses with no advice, runtime annotation or correctness assumption
- encoding: m=n^{O_ε(1)}>n depending only on n,ε and m<n^k → a deterministic function m with n<m(n)<n^k eventually; reason: k is fixed before n, so the same displayed bound already gives polynomial growth
- encoding: exp(−Ω_ε(m)) → exp(−ε²m/128) eventually; reason: the construction uses a fixed rational θ between ε/2 and ε; the source proof rate θ²/32 gives the displayed ε-rate

missions.name: A passive self-correcting quantum memory in three dimensions
missions.description:
## Motivation

A **quantum memory** stores a qubit in a many-body system. A **passive self-correcting** memory does this with no active error correction: the system is only coupled to a thermal bath at a fixed temperature, and its own Hamiltonian keeps the encoded qubit recoverable for a time that grows without bound with the system size. The classical analogue is the 2D Ising ferromagnet, whose magnetization survives thermal noise below the critical temperature. Whether a quantum analogue exists in three dimensions, with local interactions and bounded density, has been a long-standing question: the 2D and 3D toric codes are not self-correcting (see the review of [Brown et al., 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.6643)), and Haah's cubic code reaches a lifetime that grows only polynomially in the system size, up to a size cutoff set by the temperature ([Bravyi–Haah, 2013](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.3252)). [Chesi, Loss, Bravyi and Terhal (2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.2807) gave a general criterion that reduces self-correction to a statement about the Gibbs state, and the 4D toric code is self-correcting ([Alicki, Horodecki, Horodecki, Horodecki, 2010](https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.0033)).

Balasubramanian, Davydova and Lin ([arXiv:2605.10943](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10943)) construct a family of 3D-local CSS stabilizer Hamiltonians on $n_k=\exp(\Theta(k))$ qubits with one logical qubit, and show that below a critical temperature the encoded qubit survives for time $\exp(\Theta(n_k^\eta))$.

## Setting

A **CSS code** on $n$ qubits is a pair of parity-check matrices $H_x\in\mathbb F_2^{m_x\times n}$, $H_z\in\mathbb F_2^{m_z\times n}$ with $H_xH_z^T=0$. Row $a$ of $H_x$ is the $X$-type stabilizer $S^X_a=X^{(H_x)_a}$ and row $b$ of $H_z$ the $Z$-type stabilizer $S^Z_b=Z^{(H_z)_b}$, where $X^v|y\rangle=|y+v\rangle$ and $Z^w|y\rangle=(-1)^{w\cdot y}|y\rangle$. The code encodes $n-\operatorname{rank}H_x-\operatorname{rank}H_z$ logical qubits. A **syndrome** is $\sigma=(\sigma_Z,\sigma_X)$, with $\sigma_Z\in\operatorname{im}H_x$ the pattern of violated $X$-checks and $\sigma_X\in\operatorname{im}H_z$ the pattern of violated $Z$-checks; $|\sigma|$ is its Hamming weight and $\Pi_\sigma$ the projector onto the states with that syndrome.

The **stabilizer Hamiltonian** is $H=\sum_a\frac{1-S^X_a}{2}+\sum_b\frac{1-S^Z_b}{2}$, which equals $|\sigma|$ on the syndrome-$\sigma$ subspace, and the **Gibbs state** at inverse temperature $\beta=1/T$ is $\rho_\beta=e^{-\beta H}/\mathrm{Tr}\,e^{-\beta H}$. Thermal noise is modelled by the master equation $\dot\rho=-i[H,\rho]+\mathcal L(\rho)$ with **Lindbladian** $\mathcal L(\rho)=\sum_j(S_j\rho S_j^\dagger-\frac12\{\rho,S_j^\dagger S_j\})$ and evolution $\Phi_t=e^{-it[H,\cdot]+t\mathcal L}$. A jump operator is **admissible** if it is a single-qubit Pauli times a function of the syndrome, $S=P\sum_\sigma f(\sigma)\Pi_\sigma$; such Lindbladians include the Davies generators of a weakly coupled bath, and we require $\mathcal L(\rho_\beta)=0$. $\|\mathcal L\|_1$ is the operator norm of $\mathcal L$ induced by the trace norm $\|X\|_1=\mathrm{Tr}\sqrt{X^\dagger X}$.

Given logical operators $X_L=X^{x_L}$, $Z_L=Z^{z_L}$, a **decoder** $(f_Z,f_X)$ returning a Pauli correction $\mathcal O(\sigma)=X^{f_X(\sigma_X)}Z^{f_Z(\sigma_Z)}$ with syndrome $\sigma$, and an isometry $V$ onto the code space, the map $|a\rangle\otimes|\sigma\rangle\mapsto\mathcal O(\sigma)V|a\rangle$ splits the Hilbert space as $\mathcal H_{\log}\otimes\mathcal H_{\mathrm{syn}}$. The **thermal encoding** is $\mathrm{Enc}_\beta(\tau)=\tau\otimes e^{-\beta H'}/\mathrm{Tr}\,e^{-\beta H'}$ with $H'$ the syndrome weight, and **decoding** is $\mathrm{Dec}=\mathrm{Tr}_{\mathcal H_{\mathrm{syn}}}$.

**Locality in $\mathbb R^3$**: qubits get positions in $\mathbb R^3$ such that the support of every check lies in a ball of radius $r$, every unit ball contains at most $D$ qubits, and every qubit is in at most $w$ checks.

## Formalization targets

### Goal (Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, p. 4)

There are a family of CSS codes $C_k$ with one logical qubit on $n_k$ qubits, with $e^{c_1k}\le n_k\le e^{c_2k}$ for $k\ge k_0$, positions in $\mathbb R^3$ that are local with constants $r,D,w$, and constants $\beta_c,c,\eta>0$ independent of $k$, such that for every $k$ there is a decoder frame with: for every $\beta>\beta_c$, every admissible $\mathcal L$ with $\mathcal L(\rho_\beta)=0$, every single-qubit state $\tau$ and every $t\ge0$, $\mathrm{Enc}_\beta$ is CPTP, $\mathrm{Dec}\circ\mathrm{Enc}_\beta(\tau)=\tau$,

$$\bigl\|\Phi_t\circ\mathrm{Enc}_\beta(\tau)-\mathrm{Enc}_\beta(\tau)\bigr\|_1\le\|\mathcal L\|_1\,t\,e^{-c\,n_k^\eta},$$

and the distance stays $\le 1/10$ whenever $\|\mathcal L\|_1t\le e^{c\,n_k^\eta}/10$. No constant is fixed: only the shape $\exp(\Theta(n_k^\eta))$ is asserted.

The paper's eq. (5) defines the lifetime as $t_{\mathrm{mem}}=\min\{t:\|\cdots\|_1\le 1/10\}$. Read literally this is $0$ for every code, since the distance is $0$ at $t=0$, so the stated bound $t_{\mathrm{mem}}\ge\exp(\Theta(n_k^\eta))$ would be false. The goal uses the intended definition, the first time the distance exceeds $1/10$. This correction is marked in the goal's title.

### Milestones

1. **Homological perturbation lemma** (Appendix A, eqs. (244)–(247)) over $\mathbb F_2$, under the nilpotence condition $(h\delta)^N=0$.
2. **Lemma 3.3**: for degree bounds $(z_v,z_e)$ there is $t'$ such that for every $t$ there is $\ell>1$ for which every square complex with a $(t,1)$-embedding in $\mathbb R^3$ also has a $(t',\ell)$-embedding.
3. **Theorem 2.6** (Chesi–Loss–Bravyi–Terhal): $\|e^{-it[H,\cdot]+\mathcal Lt}\mathrm{Enc}(\tau)-\mathrm{Enc}(\tau)\|_1\le8\|\mathcal L\|_1t\,\mathrm{Tr}(1-P_{\mathrm{stable}})\rho_\beta$.
4. **Lemma 5.9**: at most $|V_2|(\Delta+1)^{2m}$ connected $m$-vertex sets meet $V_2$ in a graph of maximum degree $\Delta$.
5. **Peierls estimate** (eqs. (218)–(220)): $\mathbb P_\beta(\tau\subseteq\sigma)\le e^{-\beta|\tau|}$ for the Gibbs distribution on coboundaries.

## Significance

The goal gives a three-dimensional, local, bounded-density Hamiltonian whose Gibbs dynamics preserves a qubit for a time stretched-exponential in the system size, below a constant critical temperature and uniformly over admissible thermal Lindbladians. It answers the existence question for 3D passive quantum memories in the stabilizer setting, under the paper's model of thermal noise. Downstream, it bears on the thermal stability of topological order and on whether low-temperature Gibbs states of 3D local Hamiltonians can be hard to prepare.

The result is proved in the paper; nothing in it has been machine-checked. The mission states the headline theorem without its construction, so any family that satisfies it counts. The five milestones are generic tools that apply beyond this paper: the perturbation lemma for transferring homology, the embedding lemma for bounded-degree complexes, the Chesi–Loss–Bravyi–Terhal criterion, which reduces memory lifetime to a Gibbs-state estimate, and the counting and energy estimates of the Peierls argument.

## Difficulty

The obvious approach is to take a code family known to have a macroscopic energy barrier and apply the memory criterion. This does not work. An energy barrier alone does not control the entropy of low-energy error configurations, and Peierls-type counting needs every unstable syndrome to contain a witness whose energy grows with its size. In addition the codes must stay local with bounded density in $\mathbb R^3$ at every scale, while their checks must expand enough for the witness energy to grow. The paper's codes are built by iterated replacement of squares and re-embedded at every level by a random perturbation, so that local checks and bounded density survive all levels. The decoder is a renormalization-group procedure whose stability must be proved level by level. Formalizing the goal requires the construction (§3), the decoder (§4) and the witness structure (§5), none of which is stated in this mission.

## Formalization scope

Qubits are indexed by bit strings $\mathrm{Fin}\,n\to\mathbb Z/2$, with bit $0$ the state $|0\rangle$. Operators are complex matrices over that index, $Y_q=iX_qZ_q$, and $\sigma_Z(a)=1$ means that $S^X_a$ has eigenvalue $-1$. $H$ has one term $(1-S)/2$ per row of $H_x$ and of $H_z$, including redundant rows. The evolution is the matrix exponential of the generator written on vectorized operators. The trace norm is the platform's `WildeQIT.traceNorm`, and $\|\mathcal L\|_1$ is the least $c\ge0$ with $\|\mathcal L X\|_1\le c\|X\|_1$. Balls are closed. Positions need not be injective. A square's image is two triangles along a diagonal.

Taking the jump operators literally in the set of single-qubit Paulis would make the goal vacuous: such Lindbladians are unital, and for $\beta\ne0$ the condition $\mathcal L(\rho_\beta)=0$ then forces $\mathcal L=0$. Hence the class "Pauli times syndrome function". The decoder frame is fixed for each $k$ before $\beta$ and $\mathcal L$, the constants come before $k$, and the qubit-degree bound rules out padding a code with duplicated checks.

A complete development needs CSS codes and their syndrome calculus, the Chesi–Loss–Bravyi–Terhal criterion (milestone 3, reusable for any stabilizer memory), cochain complexes and the perturbation lemma (milestone 1), the embedding lemma (milestone 2), Peierls counting (milestones 4–5), and the paper's construction and RG decoder. Contributions to any milestone, or to the trace-norm and Lindbladian infrastructure, are welcome.

## Selected references

- S. Balasubramanian, M. Davydova, T.-C. Lin, *A passive self-correcting quantum memory in three dimensions*, preprint, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10943
- S. Chesi, D. Loss, S. Bravyi, B. M. Terhal, *Thermodynamic stability criteria for a quantum memory based on stabilizer and subsystem codes*, New J. Phys. 12, 025013, 2010. https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.2807
- R. Alicki, M. Horodecki, P. Horodecki, R. Horodecki, *On thermal stability of topological qubit in Kitaev's 4D model*, Open Syst. Inf. Dyn. 17, 1–20, 2010. https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.0033
- S. Bravyi, J. Haah, *Quantum self-correction in the 3D cubic code model*, Phys. Rev. Lett. 111, 200501, 2013. https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.3252
- B. J. Brown, D. Loss, J. K. Pachos, C. N. Self, J. R. Wootton, *Quantum memories at finite temperature*, Rev. Mod. Phys. 88, 045005, 2016. https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.6643
- M. Crainic, *On the perturbation lemma, and deformations*, 2004. https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0403266

main_theorem.theorem_title: Theorem 1.1 + 1.2 — a 3D-local CSS stabilizer Hamiltonian family is a self-correcting quantum memory (corrected: t_mem uses "> 1/10")
main_theorem.formal_statement:
namespace SelfCorrect3D.Memory

/-- **Theorems 1.1 and 1.2: a passive self-correcting quantum memory in three dimensions**
(corrected: `t_mem` uses "> 1/10"). Balasubramanian, Davydova, Lin, *A passive self-correcting quantum memory in three dimensions*, arXiv:2605.10943, Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.2,
p. 4; formal version Theorem 3.16, p. 40; setting of §2.5, pp. 19–21.

There are a family of CSS codes `C_k` on `n_k` qubits, qubit positions in ℝ³ and constants
`r, D, w, c₁, c₂ > 0, k₀, β_c > 0, c > 0, η > 0`, independent of `k`, such that
1. `e^{c₁k} ≤ n_k ≤ e^{c₂k}` for `k ≥ k₀` (`n_k = exp(Θ(k))`);
2. every `C_k` encodes exactly one logical qubit;
3. every `C_k` is local in ℝ³ with radius `r`, has at most `D` qubits per unit ball and at most `w`
   checks per qubit;
4. for every `k` there are logicals, a decoder and a code isometry `F` such that for every
   `β > β_c` and every Lindbladian `𝓛` of admissible jump operators with `𝓛(ρ_β) = 0`: the thermal
   encoding `Enc_β` is CPTP, and for every single-qubit density matrix `τ`,
   (a) `Dec(Enc_β(τ)) = τ`, and for every `t ≥ 0`
   (b) `‖Φ_t(Enc_β τ) − Enc_β τ‖₁ ≤ ‖𝓛‖₁ t e^{−c n_k^η}`,
   (c) if `‖𝓛‖₁ t ≤ e^{c n_k^η}/10` then `‖Φ_t(Enc_β τ) − Enc_β τ‖₁ ≤ 1/10`,
   where `Φ_t = e^{−it[H_k,·] + t𝓛}`.

**Formalization Note.** Readings, all recorded in the item's differences list: (1) admissible
jump operators are `P · F`, `P` a single-qubit Pauli, `F` a syndrome function
(`IsAdmissibleJump`), with stationary `ρ_β`; (2) the rate dependence is explicit through
`‖𝓛‖₁` (`superNorm` of the dissipator), with `β_c, c, η` independent of `𝓛`; (3) `Θ(·)` and
`O(1)` become explicit constants independent of `k`; (4) `Enc_k`, `Dec_k` are the thermal
encoding (49) and partial trace in the frame `F`, fixed per `k` before `β` and `𝓛`; (5) the
qubit-degree bound is an extra conjunct; (6) `T < T_c` is `β > β_c = 1/T_c`; positions are a map
`Fin n_k → ℝ³` and a Hamiltonian term is a row of `H_x` or `H_z`. (Correction) Eq. (5) defines
`t_mem = min{t : ‖…‖₁ ≤ 1/10}`, which is `0` for every code (the distance is `0` at `t = 0`);
clause (c) states the intended lifetime bound ("the timescale when the encoded state is
forgotten", i.e. the first time the distance exceeds `1/10`). -/
theorem exists_3d_self_correcting_memory :
    ∃ (n mX mZ : ℕ → ℕ) (C : ∀ k, CSSCode (n k) (mX k) (mZ k))
      (pos : ∀ k, Fin (n k) → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3))
      (r : ℝ) (D w : ℕ) (c₁ c₂ : ℝ) (k₀ : ℕ) (βc c η : ℝ),
      0 < c₁ ∧ 0 < c₂ ∧ 0 < βc ∧ 0 < c ∧ 0 < η ∧
      (∀ k ≥ k₀, Real.exp (c₁ * k) ≤ n k ∧ (n k : ℝ) ≤ Real.exp (c₂ * k)) ∧
      (∀ k, (C k).OneLogicalQubit) ∧
      (∀ k, IsLocal (C k) (pos k) r ∧ HasDensity (pos k) D ∧ QubitDegreeLE (C k) w) ∧
      ∀ k, ∃ F : MemoryFrame (C k), ∀ β : ℝ, βc < β →
        ∀ (m : ℕ) (J : Fin m → Op (n k)), (∀ j, IsAdmissibleJump (C k) (J j)) →
          dissipator J ((C k).gibbsState β) = 0 →
          IsCPTP (encoding (C k) F β) ∧
          ∀ τ : Matrix (ZMod 2) (ZMod 2) ℂ, τ.PosSemidef → τ.trace = 1 →
            decoding (C k) F (encoding (C k) F β τ) = τ ∧
            ∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t →
              WildeQIT.traceNorm (evolution (C k).hamiltonian J t (encoding (C k) F β τ) -
                  encoding (C k) F β τ) ≤
                superNorm (dissipator J) * t * Real.exp (-(c * (n k : ℝ) ^ η)) ∧
              (superNorm (dissipator J) * t ≤ Real.exp (c * (n k : ℝ) ^ η) / 10 →
                WildeQIT.traceNorm (evolution (C k).hamiltonian J t (encoding (C k) F β τ) -
                  encoding (C k) F β τ) ≤ 1 / 10) := by sorry

end SelfCorrect3D.Memory
main_theorem.natural_language_statement:
There exist a family of CSS codes $C_k$ ($k\in\mathbb N$) on $n_k$ qubits, positions of their qubits in $\mathbb R^3$, and constants $r$, $D$, $w$, $c_1,c_2>0$, $k_0$, $\beta_c>0$, $c>0$, $\eta>0$, all independent of $k$, such that:

1. $e^{c_1k}\le n_k\le e^{c_2k}$ for all $k\ge k_0$, i.e. $n_k=\exp(\Theta(k))$;
2. every $C_k$ encodes exactly one logical qubit;
3. every $C_k$ is local in $\mathbb R^3$: each Hamiltonian term is supported in a ball of radius $r$, every unit ball contains at most $D$ qubits, and every qubit is in at most $w$ checks;
